scenario: AITA for 'stealing' my Dad's business idea and making a success of it? | Title says it all really. I (26M) technically ''stole'' my dad's business idea. When I first heard it from him, it was so simple yet so...genius. I can't say exactly what it is here, but it was genius. The thing is, me and my dad (55M) are complete opposites. He's the more introverted and quiet type. He's always been *very* intelligent, but he's lacked the ability to *get things done.* I've been told I'm more like my grandad (75M, my dad's dad). Physically, I look more like my grandad, but personality wise, I guess I'm a bit more impulsive and hot headed and not as intelligent as my dad, but I get things done. Perhaps I'm more ''traditional masculine'' than my dad. Its like I should be in the older generation, and he should be from the newer one. When I heard my Dad's business idea, I was amazed, but I didn't truly believe my Dad could pull it off. He doesn't get things done. He's always been full of great ideas, but ideas not put to use are useless. So I took the idea and ran with it. I got IP rights and started the business with it 2 years ago. Since then, its been a massive success. Not millions or anything, but into the six figures and the potential to make millions is there perhaps in the next half decade if things keep going well. My dad was very upset when I did this, but didn't say much. I could tell by his facial expressions. My mom (55F) said I've done her proud and done the right thing. Well I confronted my dad yesterday to ask him how he feels and he said I'm a ''fucking asshole''. He said he felt betrayed by me and nearly started crying. I told him straight, ''You've always been a man of ideas, but I'm a man of action''. Then my sister (28F) walks in and starts saying shit to me, defending my dad. Both my mom and granddad have taken my side. I even offered my dad 20% of all profits, but he rejected and told me to get out. I understand why he's upset, but I think he's being unreasonable here. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I'm in the right or wrong here. Let me start by laying out the situation as I see it. My dad came up with this business idea, and when I heard it, I was really impressed. It was simple yet genius. But I didn't think he could pull it off because he's more of an ideas person but not so good at executing them. I mean, he's intelligent, but he lacks the drive to get things done. I, on the other hand, am more action-oriented. I took his idea, got the IP rights, and started the business two years ago. It's been a massive success, making six figures and with the potential to make millions in the next few years. When I first did this, my dad was upset but didn't say much. My mom was proud and thought I did the right thing. I confronted him recently, and he called me a "fucking asshole," saying he felt betrayed and almost cried. I told him he's a man of ideas and I'm a man of action. My sister sided with him, but my mom and granddad support me. I even offered him 20% of the profits, but he rejected it and told me to get out. I understand his feelings, but I think he's being unreasonable. I mean, I took his idea and turned it into something successful. Shouldn't he be proud? Or is it wrong to take his idea without his consent? Hmm, maybe I should consider the ethical side. Did I steal his idea? Or was it more about taking an idea that he wasn't going to act on and making it work? I think the key here is whether he had any intention or ability to pursue the idea himself. If he wasn't going to do anything with it, then maybe I wasn't stealing but just using an unused resource. But on the other hand, ideas are personal, and taking someone else's idea without their permission could be seen as wrong, even if they weren't going to act on it. Also, the emotional aspect is important. My dad felt betrayed, which is a strong reaction. Even if I thought he wouldn't pursue the idea, taking it without his consent hurt him. Maybe I should have talked to him first or at least discussed it before moving forward. That way, he might have felt included or at least respected. But then again, I'm the one who put in the work and made it successful. I took the risk, invested time and resources, and turned it into a business. So, in a way, it's my success, even if the idea came from him. But does that mean I should share the profits with him, or is it enough that I used his idea? I offered him 20%, which is a significant share, but he refused. Maybe he's more upset about the principle of me taking his idea rather than the money. Or perhaps he feels that I disrespected him by not involving him in the process. I also need to think about the family dynamics. My mom and granddad support me, but my sister is on my dad's side. This could create tension in the family, which is something I should consider. Maybe I should have handled it differently to maintain family harmony. Another angle is the legal aspect. I got the IP rights, so legally, I own the idea now. But legally owning it doesn't necessarily mean it's ethically right. There's a difference between what's legally permissible and what's morally correct. So, even if I have the legal rights, I might still be in the wrong morally if I took the idea without his consent. I also wonder about the potential consequences. If I continue without reconciling with my dad, it could lead to long-term issues in our relationship. Is the success of the business worth damaging my relationship with my dad? That's a tough question. On the other hand, if I had asked for his permission or involved him from the start, maybe he wouldn't have been so upset. But I didn't, and now I'm dealing with the fallout. So, maybe I should have communicated better from the beginning. In summary, I took my dad's idea, turned it into a successful business, but hurt his feelings in the process. Legally, I'm in the clear, but morally, it's more complicated. I need to balance the success I've achieved with the emotional impact on my dad and the family dynamics. Perhaps I should find a way to reconcile with him, even if it means giving him a share of the business or just apologizing for not involving him.
